data.title: Alphabet sells C$6B of bonds, a 40-year at 6%, at wider spreads than its May deal
data.description:
Alphabet has sold C$6.0 billion of Canadian dollar bonds, including a 40-year note that pays 6.000% a year, according to a pricing term sheet the company filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday, November 20, 2026. The sale was priced on Thursday, at wider spreads than Alphabet paid in the same market in May. It is worth about US$4.2 billion at the Bank of Canada's exchange rate for that day.

The deal adds to a year of heavy borrowing. Alphabet's long-term debt rose from $46.5 billion to $125.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, its quarterly report shows, and in June it raised another $49.5 billion by selling common and preferred stock. The cash flow statement shows where the pressure comes from. Last quarter the company spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures and brought in $42.3 billion from its operations, TECHi's reading of the filing shows.

What did Alphabet sell?

Four series of senior unsecured notes, all in Canadian dollars. Bonds sold in that currency by foreign companies are known as maple bonds. The term sheet lists C$2.0 billion due in 2029 at 4.100%, C$1.25 billion due in 2034 at 4.800%, C$1.5 billion due in 2038 at 5.325%, and C$1.25 billion due in 2066 at 6.000%.

Each was priced just below face value. The longest note was sold at a yield 1.85 percentage points above a Canadian government bond maturing in 2057. The three-year note was sold 0.75 points above the government curve.

Moody's rates the notes Aa2 and S&P rates them AA+, both with a stable outlook. RBC Dominion Securities, Scotia Capital and TD Securities ran the sale, with CIBC as co-manager. It is due to settle on November 24, and interest will be paid twice a year. Alphabet can redeem any of the series early, at a price tied to Canadian government yields.

Interest on the four series comes to C$296.9 million a year, about US$207 million. The banks' fees are C$18.1 million, and Alphabet receives C$5.97 billion before its own expenses.

One part of the plan is missing. The preliminary document Alphabet filed on Thursday morning described five series, one of them paying a floating rate. The final terms list four, all at fixed rates. The filings do not say why.

Is Alphabet paying more to borrow?

Yes, on the evidence of its own term sheets. This is the company's second sale of Canadian dollar bonds in six months. The first, priced on May 5, raised C$8.5 billion in four series through the same three banks.

Bond investors measure the cost of a company's debt by its spread, the extra yield over a government bond of similar life. In May Alphabet's seven-year notes were sold 0.60 percentage points over the Canadian government curve, and its ten-year notes 0.75 points over. This week its eight-year notes were sold 1.15 points over and its 12-year notes 1.45 points over. The three-year notes in the new sale carry the same spread, 0.75 points, as the ten-year notes did in May.

The longest notes give the cleanest comparison, because both sales were priced against the same Canadian government bond, due in December 2057. In May Alphabet's 30-year notes yielded 1.10 points more than that bond. Its new 40-year notes yield 1.85 points more. The government bond's own yield rose by less than 0.2 points between the two sales, from 3.963% to 4.151%.

The new notes run somewhat longer, which accounts for part of the difference. But an eight-year note at 1.15 points against a seven-year note at 0.60 is a wide gap for one extra year.

Weighted by size, the May sale carried an average coupon of 4.35% over an average life of 14.9 years. The new one carries 4.95% over 14.0 years.

It is not Alphabet's longest debt. The debt table in its quarterly report lists sterling notes that mature in 2126, the 100-year bond TECHi wrote about when it was sold.

How much has Alphabet borrowed this year?

A great deal, in seven currencies. In the nine months to September 30 the company issued $45.0 billion of US dollar notes and $35.8 billion of notes in other currencies, the quarterly report says. Those were sold in euros, sterling, Swiss francs, Canadian dollars, yen and Australian dollars.

In the third quarter alone Alphabet sold $25.1 billion of US dollar notes with an average coupon of 5.55% and an average maturity of 15 years. It also sold A$5.6 billion of Australian dollar notes at an average of 5.82% over eight years.

The face value of its long-term debt went from $49.1 billion at the end of 2025 to $127.5 billion at the end of September. That is 2.6 times as much, an increase of $78.4 billion.

Debt was only part of it. On June 4 Alphabet sold 29 million Class A shares at $355.20 and 29 million Class C shares at $351.80, raising $20.5 billion. The same day it sold $10.0 billion of stock privately to an affiliate of Berkshire Hathaway. A day later it raised $19.0 billion through preferred stock that pays 6.25% and converts into common shares.

Added together, Alphabet raised $130.3 billion from investors in nine months: $80.8 billion in notes and $49.5 billion in stock.

It has kept going since. On November 2 it priced €6.0 billion of euro notes, about $6.7 billion at the European Central Bank's rate for that day. This week's sale adds about $4.2 billion. That takes the year's total to at least $141 billion.

Where is the money going?

Into data centers and the equipment inside them. Capital expenditures were $132.0 billion in the first nine months of 2026, against $63.6 billion a year earlier. The company says the spending mainly reflects investment in technical infrastructure, and that the June proceeds would be used for purposes including capital expenditures to scale AI infrastructure.

That is more than the business generated. Cash from operations was $127.1 billion over the same nine months, $4.8 billion less than the capital spending. In the third quarter alone the gap was $9.1 billion.

Alphabet is not short of cash. It held $265.1 billion of cash and marketable securities at the end of September, up from $126.8 billion at the start of the year, and that is $140 billion more than its long-term debt. It has been raising money faster than it spends it. A commercial paper program of up to $25.0 billion and $10.0 billion of bank credit lines were both unused at the end of the quarter.

What does the debt cost?

More than it used to, though still less than Alphabet earns on its own cash. Interest expense was $967 million in the third quarter, 6.8 times the $143 million of a year earlier. That figure is after $405 million of interest was capitalized, meaning added to the cost of assets under construction instead of being charged against profit. Over nine months interest expense was $2.78 billion, against $438 million a year earlier.

Interest income on its cash was $1.77 billion in the quarter, so Alphabet still earned more on its savings than it paid on its debt.

The new notes add about US$207 million a year. The US dollar notes it sold in 2020 carry coupons of 0.80% to 2.25%. Those it sold in 2026 carry 3.70% to 6.50%.

What does it mean for Alphabet stock?

There are two ways to read it. The ratings are among the highest any company holds, the cash pile exceeds the debt, and lenders will still give Alphabet money for 40 years. Borrowing on those terms to pay for data centers is what a strong balance sheet allows.

Against that, capital spending now exceeds the cash the business produces, the difference is being met by outside money, and that money costs more than it did in May. The shares sold in June at $355.20 were trading at $272.22 at 1:16 p.m. Eastern on Friday, 23.4% lower. They were down 0.2% on the day. The investors who bought then are behind, and a further sale of stock at today's price would be on worse terms for the company.

This week the market has treated the buyers of AI hardware better than the sellers. Alphabet's market value passed Nvidia's on Friday, as TECHi reported.

What to watch

Settlement on November 24. Alphabet's next quarterly results will show whether capital spending again exceeded operating cash flow and what it plans for 2027. Any return of the floating-rate notes that were left out of this sale, and any further issue of debt or stock before the year ends. TECHi's Alphabet quote page carries the live price.

data.title: TSMC's US premium over its Taipei shares falls to 5.0% after Friday's slide
data.description:
TSMC's American shares have lost most of the premium they usually carry over the company's shares in Taipei. Each US-listed share represents five Taiwan shares, and it closed on Friday, November 20, 2026 at $318.71, Nasdaq data show, down 9.5% on the day. That left it worth 5.0% more than the five underlying shares at their last Taipei close, TECHi's calculation from exchange and central bank data shows. Over the past two years the gap has averaged about 18.6%.

Taipei had its first chance to react on Monday, November 23, and the shares closed at NT$2,030, up 1.5% from Friday, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange. New curbs on short selling took effect in Taiwan the same morning. In Seoul the main index fell 3.3%, while US stock-index futures pointed to a rebound in New York.

What is the premium, and how far has it fallen?

It is the extra that investors in New York pay for TSMC compared with investors in Taipei. The company's American depositary shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange in dollars. Each one stands for five ordinary shares, which trade on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in New Taiwan dollars. Convert the Taipei price at the central bank's closing rate for the Taiwan dollar, multiply by five, and the result can be set against the ADR price.

The premium is not a fee, and no one collects it. It is the difference between the prices at which buyers and sellers in two markets are willing to trade, and it can change without either price being wrong.

The ADR has cost more for as long as the data TECHi checked goes back, to August 2024. Across 544 trading days the premium ranged from 3.6% to 33.5%, with a median of 18.6%. Over the past year the median was 15.9%. In October it was 15.3%.

Friday's figure, 5.0%, is the second-lowest in that period. The only lower reading came on November 5, at 3.6%.

The slide has been fast. A week earlier, on November 13, the premium was 11.4%. On Thursday it was 10.5%. Most of the drop came on Friday, when the ADR fell 9.5% and Taipei, whose session had ended before New York opened, did not trade again until Monday.

Why did New York fall harder than Taipei?

Partly timing, and partly who was selling. Taipei's Friday session closed at 12:30 a.m. Eastern time, nine hours before trading began in New York. The heaviest selling in US chip stocks came during the New York session that followed, as TECHi reported on Friday.

Over the whole week the gap is plain. The ADR fell 20.1% from its close on November 13. The Taipei shares fell 14.9% over the same five sessions, even though Taiwan's main index, the Taiex, dropped 17.5%, its worst week in exchange data going back to July 2024.

Measured from their highs the difference is larger still. The ADR's best close was $485.80 on October 5, and Friday's price is 34.4% below it. The Taipei shares peaked at NT$2,585 on October 6 and on Friday were 22.6% lower.

Who sold cannot be read from prices. What the numbers show is that US investors were willing to pay much less for TSMC on Friday, relative to Taipei, than at any time in the past two years except one day earlier this month.

What happened in Taipei on Monday?

The market opened lower and recovered. TSMC closed at NT$2,030, up 1.5% from Friday. It traded as low as NT$1,970 before recovering. The Taiex rose 2.2% by the close.

The rise came after a report over the weekend. Nikkei Asia reported on Sunday, citing an unnamed source, that TSMC had paused some shipments to Chinese chip designers, according to an account of the report by Tom's Hardware. The new US export rule asks chipmakers to treat chips made at 16 or 14 nanometers or finer as controlled unless their designers document their performance, that account says. TECHi could not read the original report, and the account does not include a response from TSMC.

Monday was the first day of new rules. On Saturday, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission announced five measures from November 23. Investors may not sell listed shares short below the previous day's closing price, with an exception for hedging by brokers and futures firms. The minimum margin on short sales rises to 150% from 130%. Applications to issue new put warrants are suspended. The commission also encouraged listed companies to buy back their own shares and asked lenders to stop lending shares out and to recall loans where contracts allow.

At Monday's Taipei close and the current exchange rate of 32.871 Taiwan dollars per US dollar, five TSMC shares are worth $308.78. Friday's ADR close is 3.2% above that.

What does that mean for the ADR when New York opens?

The premium has to land somewhere, and where it lands sets the ADR price. TECHi's arithmetic, at Monday's Taipei close, shows three cases. If the premium stayed at Friday's 5.0%, the ADR would be worth about $324. At November's median of 11.5% it would be about $344. At the two-year median of 18.6% it would be about $366.

These are not forecasts. The premium has no fixed level, and the ADR will trade on whatever New York investors decide on Monday.

There is a recent example of how fast it can move. After the premium fell to 3.6% on November 5, it was back at 15.2% a day later. Both markets moved: the ADR rose 6.3% on November 6, and the Taipei shares fell 4.7%.

Early signals point to a higher open in New York. In Friday's after-hours trading the ADR changed hands at $328.60, 6.4% above Monday's Taipei value. Nasdaq-100 futures were up 2.8% at 1:22 a.m. Eastern time on Monday, after the Nasdaq-100 index fell 5.6% on Friday, and S&P 500 futures were up 2.0%.

What happened in Seoul?

A second day of heavy selling. The Korea Composite Stock Price Index closed down 3.3% from Friday's close, according to Korea Exchange prices published by Naver Finance. Samsung Electronics fell 1.9% and SK hynix fell 1.4%. Both supply memory chips used in AI servers, and their moves are watched in New York as a read on Micron.

The Korea Exchange suspended program trading for five minutes on Monday morning, the second session in a row it has done so, Yonhap reported. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said the government had a contingency plan beyond a market stabilization fund that the authorities agreed on Sunday to prepare, but he was cautious about using the fund, saying a decision would follow a close review of the market, the news agency reported. The fund was last used after the 2008 financial crisis.

The selling came on the same morning that Korea's customs data showed chip exports in the first 20 days of November nearly quadrupling from a year earlier, to a record $38.5 billion, according to Yonhap.

What does it mean for TSMC shareholders?

It depends on which market they hold. For Taipei shareholders, Monday's close leaves the stock near where Friday ended, under new rules that limit short selling. For ADR holders, Friday's loss was larger, and part of it was a loss of premium that Taipei never matched.

The premium has been shrinking for months. Its monthly median was above 20% in nine months of 2025 and has been between 11% and 16% in each month since July. Friday's reading took it far below that.

There is a case that it comes back. It has rebounded quickly before, and the futures market pointed higher on Sunday night. There is also a case that it does not. A premium is a measure of how much extra demand there is in New York, and that demand fell sharply last week.

What to watch

The ADR's first trade on Monday, and where it leaves the premium. Whether Taipei holds its level on Tuesday after the ADR has traded. Any decision in Seoul to use the stabilization fund. TECHi's TSMC quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; shares jump 29%, adding about $876 billion
data.description:
Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately, the company said at 8:55 a.m. Eastern on Monday, November 23, 2026. The decision came 12 days after the board accepted his resignation and six days after its chair said it did not intend to bring him back. The board voted unanimously after a series of meetings with Huang left it satisfied with his candor and his ability to lead the company, Nvidia said in a statement filed with the SEC.

Investors reacted within a minute. Nvidia's shares were at $136.00 in pre-market trading at 8:54 a.m. and $149.56 at 8:55, Nasdaq data show, and they were up 28.9% at $161.87 at 9:50 a.m. That adds about $876 billion to Nvidia's market value since Friday's close and recovers 75% of the roughly $1.16 trillion it lost between November 11 and Friday, TECHi's calculation shows.

What did Nvidia's board decide?

To undo the change at the top. The board reinstated Huang on November 22, according to the company's filing, and announced it the next morning. Colette Kress, who served as interim chief executive, continues as chief financial officer, and Harvey Jones remains chair. The board believes Huang is "the right person to lead NVIDIA," Jones said in the statement.

The statement also says the board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and that on the basis of that input it is confident Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk. It does not say who gave that input or when.

Why did the board change its mind?

The statement points to two things: its own meetings with Huang and the government's input. It gives no other reason. On November 17, Jones opened Nvidia's earnings call by saying the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, as TECHi reported from accounts of the call. The board had hired a search firm and was looking at candidates from inside and outside the company.

Outside pressure pointed both ways around that statement. Two days before it, on November 15, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged the board to hire from outside. On Sunday night President Donald Trump wrote that he hoped the board would rehire Huang, as TECHi reported this morning. The filing dates the board's decision to November 22, the same day as Trump's post, which went up at 9:54 p.m. Eastern. Nvidia does not say whether the decision came before or after it. Nvidia's statements in the week of the resignation gave no reason for it, and Monday's statement does not describe what the board learned in its meetings with Huang.

What happens to the search and the board?

The statement does not mention the search for a permanent chief executive, for which the board hired Heidrick & Struggles last week, and does not say whether it has ended. With Huang back as a director, the board returns to 11 members from the 10 who remained after he left, as TECHi counted at the time.

The timing also lands two days before the date by which Bessent said he wanted answers from the board and its outside counsel. The decision matches the hope the President expressed on Sunday and runs against the Treasury Secretary's call for an outsider.

What has not changed?

The investigations. The statement says the committee of independent directors examining recent reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort will continue its work to conclusion, and that Huang supports it. Its national security and export control committee, set up last week as TECHi reported, is engaging counsel with national security experience.

Nvidia is also starting a search for a new chief compliance officer, who will report to the board's nominating and corporate governance committee. Its proxy statement in May said it had no such post. The company says it will keep cooperating with government investigations and inquiries. Reuters reported on Friday that the Securities and Exchange Commission is examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia, as TECHi reported; Nvidia has not confirmed that inquiry.

How did the shares react?

Fast. From $136.00 at 8:54 a.m. to $149.56 a minute later, a 10.0% jump, and to $162.36 by 9:13 a.m., Nasdaq data show. In those 19 minutes Nvidia's market value rose by about $635 billion on its 24.1 billion shares.

At 9:50 a.m. the shares were at $161.87, up 28.9% from Friday's close of $125.53, using the median of the last five one-minute prints to smooth out single trades. That still leaves the shares 6.8% below their close of $173.73 on November 11, the day the board accepted Huang's resignation, and 13.3% below their $186.64 close on November 6.

The move is larger than the one that greeted his departure. On November 12, the day Nvidia announced the resignation, the shares opened 13.1% lower at $151.01 and recovered to close at $166.19, down 4.3%, as TECHi reported then. Investors marked the stock down far less for Huang's exit than they marked it up for his return, though the week in between also brought the reported SEC inquiry and the steepest weekly fall for AI hardware stocks in TECHi's records.

What did it do to other AI stocks?

It lifted them further. Ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks were up 12.7% on average from Friday's close at 9:50 a.m., against 7.4% at 4:30 a.m., before the news, as TECHi's pre-market report showed. CoreWeave 20.7%, Dell 19.2% and Super Micro 17.9% led the group. Many of these companies sell to Nvidia, build servers around its chips or depend on them, so its leadership matters to them as well.

Where does that leave Nvidia against Alphabet?

Back in front. Nvidia's market value fell below Alphabet's on Friday afternoon, as TECHi reported. At 9:50 a.m. Nvidia was worth about $3.90 trillion and Alphabet about $3.40 trillion on the share counts in its latest quarterly report, a lead of about $502 billion.

What does it mean for shareholders?

There are two readings, and both are in the price. One is relief: Nvidia's co-founder and longtime chief executive is back, and the board says the national security question has been answered to its satisfaction. The size of the move suggests most investors share that view.

The other is about governance. The board reversed a public decision within six days, after input from the government that it does not describe, while its own investigation and a reported SEC inquiry are still open. Investors will want to know what the investigation finds and whether the new compliance officer and committee change how the company is run.

For holders of Nvidia's suppliers and customers, the morning showed how closely their shares are tied to its leadership. The ten hardware stocks added to their average pre-market gain after the announcement, from 7.4% at 4:30 a.m. to 12.7% at 9:50 a.m.

What to watch

The rest of Monday's session, and whether Nvidia holds its gain. The findings of the independent committee's investigation, for which Nvidia has given no date, and the appointment of a chief compliance officer, a post its May proxy statement said it did not have. Huang's appearance before House lawmakers on December 1, which CBS News reported last week, and Nvidia's quarterly report, due by December 4. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Intuit sells Mailchimp for $3.68B, five years after paying $12B; price is 2.9x revenue
data.description:
Intuit has agreed to sell Mailchimp, its email marketing business, to the Italian technology company Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Intuit paid $12.0 billion for Mailchimp in November 2021. The sale price is 31% of that. Intuit's shares were down 10.7% at $276.99 at 2:47 p.m. Eastern on Friday, in afternoon trading, after the company also cut its revenue forecast for the year.

Intuit's own figures show what the buyer is getting. The price is 2.9 times Mailchimp's revenue last fiscal year and 6.1 times its operating profit, TECHi's calculation shows. Mailchimp's revenue is where it was two years ago, while the rest of Intuit grew 34%. One more number closes the circle. Intuit issued 10.1 million shares to buy Mailchimp. It plans to spend the cash from the sale on its own stock, and at Friday's price that cash would buy about 11.9 million.

What did Intuit announce?

Two things on the same evening: quarterly results and the sale.

The purchase agreement is dated November 19. The buyer is a US subsidiary of Bending Spoons, an Italian company that owns a portfolio of digital products. The base price is $3.68 billion in cash, subject to the usual adjustments for cash, debt and working capital.

Not all of it stays cash. Under a separate agreement, Intuit will put about $368 million of the price back into Bending Spoons' parent company in exchange for 8,818,595 new shares, which is about $41.73 a share. Intuit's results release describes the deal as $3.31 billion in cash and $368 million in stock.

The sale needs US antitrust clearance and other regulatory approvals. It does not need a vote of Intuit's shareholders and does not depend on the buyer raising finance. Intuit expects it to close early in 2027. Either side can walk away if it has not closed by August 19, 2027, with a possible three-month extension. Intuit has agreed not to compete with the business for two years.

How does the price compare with what Intuit paid?

Badly. Intuit's annual report for fiscal 2022 says it acquired Mailchimp on November 1, 2021 for total consideration of $12.0 billion. That was $5.7 billion in cash and 10.1 million Intuit shares valued at about $6.3 billion, at a share price of $625.99.

The sale price is 30.7% of that, or $8.3 billion less.

The valuation has fallen further than the price. In the nine months after the purchase, Mailchimp contributed $762 million of revenue, a rate of about $1.0 billion a year. Intuit paid roughly 12 times that. Bending Spoons is paying 2.9 times last fiscal year's revenue of $1.27 billion.

The release does not say what accounting gain or loss Intuit expects to book on the sale.

What was Mailchimp contributing?

Steady profit and no growth. Intuit began reporting Mailchimp as a separate segment in August, and on Thursday it filed three years of figures on that basis.

Mailchimp's revenue was $1.267 billion in the year to July 2024, $1.287 billion in 2025 and $1.272 billion in 2026. Over two years that is growth of 0.4%. In the quarter just reported it fell 1% to $313 million, and Intuit's forecast for this fiscal year is between a 1% decline and no change.

Profit moved the other way, because costs were cut. Segment operating income rose from $516 million to $604 million over the same two years, an increase of 17%, as segment costs fell from $751 million to $668 million. That is a margin of 47.5%. The figure leaves out corporate overheads, share-based pay and the amortization of what Intuit paid for the business.

The rest of Intuit kept growing. Revenue outside Mailchimp rose from $15.02 billion to $20.18 billion over the two years, or 34.3%. Mailchimp's share of the total fell from 7.8% to 5.9%.

What will Intuit do with the money?

Buy back its own shares. The release says Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to repurchase stock within its 2027 fiscal year, after the sale closes.

At Thursday's close of $310.02, the $3.31 billion of cash would buy 10.7 million shares, 4.0% of the 268 million used in Intuit's latest per-share figures. At Friday's reading of $276.99 it would buy 11.9 million.

That is about the number Intuit issued to buy Mailchimp in the first place. In 2021 it handed over 10.1 million shares and $5.7 billion in cash. Five years on, selling the business brings in enough cash to retire a similar number of shares, because Intuit's own share price has halved. It was $625.99 when the purchase was priced and $310.02 on Thursday.

Intuit is already a heavy buyer of its stock. It repurchased $1.5 billion in the latest quarter and has $6.4 billion of authorization left. The sale's cash is equal to a little over two quarters at that pace. The company held $5.3 billion of cash and investments at the end of October against $6.9 billion of debt.

The company's stated reason for selling is focus. It says it has built AI-based tools to help businesses find customers and get paid, and that selling Mailchimp sharpens its attention on them. That is the company's account. The figures above show a business that had stopped growing inside Intuit.

How were the quarterly results?

The rest of the company is growing. Revenue for the three months to October 31 rose 12% to $4.4 billion. The business software division, which includes QuickBooks, grew 15% to $3.1 billion, and the consumer division, which includes TurboTax and Credit Karma, grew 7% to $958 million.

Operating income rose 63% to $868 million and earnings were $2.59 a share, also up 63%. On Intuit's adjusted measure, earnings were $2.91 a share, up 56%. The chief executive said results were above the top of the company's forecast.

The outlook was cut. Intuit now expects revenue of $23.08 billion to $23.37 billion for the fiscal year, growth of 8% to 9%. In August it had forecast $23.28 billion to $23.51 billion, or 9% to 10%. The range is $198 million lower at the bottom and $147 million lower at the top.

All of the reduction is at Credit Karma. Intuit now expects that business to grow 3% to 7% this year, where in August it expected 11% to 13%. Its forecasts for the business software division, TurboTax and Mailchimp did not change, and it kept its forecast for adjusted earnings of $22.88 to $23.12 a share. The release does not explain the change at Credit Karma.

For the current quarter Intuit expects revenue growth of 6% to 7%. None of the forecasts includes the sale, and Intuit said it will update them when the deal closes.

How did the stock react?

Intuit closed at $310.02 on Thursday, down 1.0%, before the announcements. At 2:47 p.m. Eastern on Friday, in afternoon trading, it was at $276.99, down 10.7%.

Two pieces of news arrived together, so the fall cannot be put down to the sale alone. The lower revenue forecast came in the same release.

The shares had already lost 53.2% this year by Thursday's close. Friday's fall leaves them 55.8% below the price at which Intuit valued its stock in the Mailchimp purchase. At Friday's reading the company was worth about $74.2 billion on its diluted share count.

There is a case on each side. Intuit is shedding a business that had stopped growing, the cash goes to shareholders, and the rest of the company grew 15% in its main division. Against that, the sale recovers less than a third of a $12.0 billion purchase price, the revenue forecast has been cut, and the wider market for technology stocks has been falling this week.

What to watch

Regulatory clearance and the closing, which Intuit expects early in 2027. The updated forecast Intuit has promised at that point. How quickly the cash is spent on buybacks, and at what price. Any disclosure of the gain or loss on the sale in the next quarterly report.

data.title: South Korea’s chip exports nearly quadruple to a record as its chip stocks keep falling
data.description:
South Korea exported a record $38.5 billion of semiconductors in the first 20 days of November, 294.4% more than in the same period a year earlier, the Korea Customs Service said on Monday, November 23, 2026. Chips made up 49.7% of everything the country shipped abroad. On the same day, shares in the country's two big memory makers fell again: SK hynix closed 2.5% lower and Samsung Electronics 3.1% lower, Yonhap reported.

The two sets of numbers have been moving apart since June. Twenty-day chip exports have risen 51.0% since then, TECHi's reading of the agency's figures shows. SK hynix shares have lost nearly two-thirds of their value from their June peak, according to Naver Finance's daily price series. In New York, Micron, the largest US-listed memory maker, closed on Friday 51.0% below its own June high.

What did the customs data show?

A record on almost every line. Total exports for November 1 to 20 were $77.4 billion, up 101.5% from a year earlier and the highest for the first 20 days of any month. The previous high was $71.6 billion, in September. Imports were $50.3 billion, leaving a surplus of $27.1 billion.

Chips led. The agency puts semiconductor exports at $38.5 billion, up 294.4%, and their share of all exports at 49.7%, 24.3 percentage points higher than a year earlier. A year earlier chips were 25.4% of the total, the agency's chart shows, so they now account for close to half of everything Korea sells abroad, up from about a quarter. Exports of computer peripherals, which include storage, rose 330.6%. Car exports fell 5.6%.

By destination, shipments to China rose 145.6%, to the United States 142.7%, to Vietnam 85.8% and to Taiwan 149.7%, where many AI servers are assembled. China, the United States and Vietnam together took 55.5% of the total. By value, China bought $20.0 billion of Korean goods and the United States $16.4 billion, Yonhap reported.

Exports since January passed $1 trillion for the first time, at $1.008 trillion, the agency said. That is 63.2% more than a year earlier.

The figures are preliminary and count goods as they clear customs. Korea publishes them for the first 20 days of each month, before most large economies publish any trade data for that month, which is why investors in chip stocks around the world watch them.

How much of the growth is chips?

Most of it. Total exports rose by $39.0 billion from a year earlier. Chip exports rose from about $9.8 billion to $38.5 billion, an increase of about $28.7 billion. That is roughly three-quarters of the gain, TECHi's calculation shows.

Take chips out and the rest of Korea's exports still grew about 36%, a strong number on its own but a much smaller one.

Adjusted for working days the picture is the same. This year's period had 16 working days and last year's 15.5. Total exports averaged $4.84 billion a working day, against $2.48 billion, an increase of 95.2%, the agency said. Chip exports came to about $2.41 billion a working day, against about $0.63 billion a year earlier.

The agency's figures are in dollars and do not say how much of the rise comes from higher chip prices and how much from more chips.

The 20-day figures the agency publishes each month show how steep the climb has been. Chip exports in the first 20 days were $8.8 billion in June 2025, $25.5 billion in June 2026 and $38.5 billion this month. Over the first 20 days of the eleven months of 2026 so far they total $258.5 billion, about three times the $86.9 billion of the same months of 2025.

What happened to the shares?

They kept falling. The Korea Composite Stock Price Index closed 3.3% lower on Monday at 4,708.54, its lowest close since January 13, Yonhap reported. It had fallen 5.2% on Friday. Samsung Electronics fell 3.1% to 177,500 won, its third straight decline, and SK hynix 2.5% to about 1.09 million won.

For the first half of the year the shares and the exports rose together. Twenty-day chip exports went from $10.7 billion in January to $25.5 billion in June, an increase of 138%. Over the same months SK hynix's share price more than quadrupled from its first close of 2026 to its June peak, and Samsung Electronics' nearly tripled.

The bigger move is the one since June. In Naver Finance's daily series, which also counts trading on Korea's after-hours Nextrade platform, SK hynix's highest close was about 2.92 million won, on June 22. Monday's close is about 63% below it. Samsung Electronics peaked at 362,500 won on June 18 and is about 51% lower. The index itself is 48.3% below its June 22 high.

Over the same months the export figures went the other way. The first-20-day chip number was $25.5 billion in June, $34.1 billion in September and $38.5 billion now.

The government is preparing to step in. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said on Monday that the authorities had a contingency plan beyond a stock market stabilization fund they agreed on Sunday to prepare, though he was cautious about using the fund, Yonhap reported.

Why are exports and share prices moving apart?

Because they measure different things. Export figures count what was shipped in the past three weeks, at prices agreed earlier. Share prices are a bet on profits years ahead.

TECHi has not established why investors are selling, and the export data cannot answer that. There are two readings. One is that demand for memory chips in AI data centers is still rising and the shares have fallen too far. The record export figure supports that view for now.

The other is that investors expect the boom to slow, and that today's record shipments will look like a peak once new factories come on line and buyers' spending cools. Memory has gone through sharp cycles before. On that view, rising exports are the wrong thing to watch, because shipments are often at their highest just before a turn.

A third possibility is that the selling has little to do with memory demand at all. Last week's losses ran across every kind of AI hardware stock in New York, from networking to servers, and Korea's chipmakers fell with them, as TECHi reported on Friday.

The data published on Monday do not settle the question. They show that shipments were still growing, at a record pace, three weeks into November.

What does it mean for Micron?

Korea's figures are watched in New York as an early read on memory demand. Samsung and SK hynix are Micron's two largest rivals in DRAM, the memory used alongside processors in AI servers. Micron closed at $594.51 on Friday, down 13.9% on the day and 23.6% for the week.

Micron's own figures show how far the business has grown. Its revenue in the fiscal year to September 3 was $133.2 billion, and it reported a take-or-pay backlog of $134 billion, its annual report shows, as TECHi reported last week.

Its shares have fallen almost as far as Samsung's from their peak. Micron's highest close was $1,213.56 on June 25. Friday's close is 51.0% below that, while Korea's chip exports over the same months have kept rising.

For Micron shareholders the export numbers are a point in favor of demand and say nothing about margins or about the next year's orders. Micron's next quarterly report, which Nasdaq's data vendor estimates for mid-December, will be the first company figure that covers November.

What to watch

Korea's full-month trade figures for November, due at the start of December. Micron's quarterly report, expected in mid-December. Whether Seoul activates the stabilization fund. TECHi's Micron quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Zscaler brings 38% of combined ARR to the CrowdStrike deal; its holders get 15.9%
data.description:
Zscaler's last quarter as an independent company, reported on Monday morning about an hour after its sale to CrowdStrike was announced, shows how much of the combined business it would bring. In the three months to October 31, 2026, Zscaler's annual recurring revenue rose 21% to $3.88 billion and its free cash flow reached a record $416.5 million, according to its results filing. CrowdStrike's quarter ended on the same day.

Put side by side, Zscaler would account for about 38% of the two companies' combined ARR, 37.5% of their revenue and 47% of their free cash flow for that quarter, TECHi's calculation shows. Its shareholders would own about 15.9% of the combined company. The gap reflects how differently the market prices the two: CrowdStrike was valued at about 37.5 times its ARR at Friday's close, Zscaler at 8.2 times.

What did Zscaler report?

Steady growth and more cash. Revenue rose 20% to $949.3 million from $788.1 million a year earlier. ARR rose 21% to $3,882 million. Net new ARR was $111 million, which Zscaler said grew 22% once the $98 million contributed a year earlier by its purchase of Red Canary is set aside.

On an adjusted basis Zscaler earned $230.2 million from operations, 24.3% of revenue, up from 21.8%. Under standard accounting it lost $33.2 million from operations and $27.4 million overall, or 17 cents a share, against adjusted earnings of $1.23 a share, up from 96 cents. Cash from operations was $541.0 million, 57% of revenue, the same share as a year earlier. Free cash flow was $416.5 million, 44% of revenue, against 52% a year earlier. Remaining performance obligations, the contracted revenue not yet recognized, rose 23% to $7.29 billion, and the company held $3.89 billion in cash and short-term investments.

Why is there no forecast?

Because of the deal. Zscaler said it would not hold its scheduled conference call and is withdrawing its previously issued financial guidance as a result of the agreement with CrowdStrike. That leaves its investors without the company's own view of the year, at a time when the fixed exchange ratio already ties Zscaler's share price to CrowdStrike's.

How do the two quarters compare?

CrowdStrike grows faster; Zscaler turns more of its revenue into cash. In the same three months CrowdStrike's revenue rose 28% to $1.58 billion and its ARR 27% to $6.26 billion, according to its own results. Its free cash flow of $474 million was 30% of revenue, against 44% at Zscaler.

Added together, the two companies had about $10.14 billion of ARR at the end of October, in line with the more than $10 billion the companies said the combined business would start with.

What else is in Zscaler's numbers?

A slower pace of new business. Zscaler added $111 million of net new ARR in the quarter, against CrowdStrike's $419.2 million, so it brought about 21% of the new recurring revenue the two added, roughly half its 38% share of the total. That slower pace is one reason investors may pay less for each of its dollars.

It also brings a strong balance sheet. Its $3.89 billion of cash and short-term investments is about $2.17 billion more than the $1.725 billion of convertible notes listed in the merger agreement. Its contracted but unrecognized revenue of $7.29 billion is about 1.9 times its ARR.

Why do Zscaler's holders get only 15.9%?

Because the split follows market value, not revenue. At Friday's closing prices, on the latest reported share counts, CrowdStrike was worth about $235 billion and Zscaler about $32.0 billion, so Zscaler was about 12.0% of the two together. The 34% premium lifts that to about 15.4% on the same share counts. The companies put the figure at 15.9% in the announcement, which does not give the share counts behind it.

What the market pays for is growth. Each dollar of CrowdStrike's ARR was valued at about $37.50 on Friday and each dollar of Zscaler's at about $8.20. CrowdStrike's ARR grows 6 points a year faster, and CrowdStrike says its growth has accelerated for five quarters in a row. The difference in valuation is far larger than the difference in growth, which is why a business that brings nearly half the cash flow gets less than a sixth of the shares.

How did the gap open?

Over the past year. On November 20, 2025, Zscaler closed at $279.73 and CrowdStrike at $125.33, adjusted for CrowdStrike's four-for-one split, Nasdaq data show. On the share counts each reported at the time, Zscaler was worth about $44.6 billion and CrowdStrike about $126.4 billion, so Zscaler was about 26% of the two together. By Friday its shares had fallen 30.4% while CrowdStrike's had risen 83.1%, and its weight had fallen to 12.0%.

Most of that change came from the price the market put on each dollar of recurring revenue rather than from the businesses. Zscaler's ARR grew 21% over the year and CrowdStrike's 27%. But CrowdStrike's market value per dollar of ARR rose from about 25.6 times to 37.5 times, on its ARR a year earlier implied by that growth rate, while Zscaler's fell from about 13.9 times to 8.2 times. Since the end of 2025, CrowdStrike's shares have risen 95.8% and Zscaler's have fallen 13.4%.

That matters for the terms. An all-stock deal fixes the exchange at current relative prices, so Zscaler's holders are swapping into CrowdStrike after a year in which the gap between the two valuations widened sharply.

Is it a good trade for Zscaler's holders?

It depends on what CrowdStrike's shares are worth. In exchange for a business growing ARR at 21%, they get a premium and a stake in one growing at 27%. If the market keeps valuing CrowdStrike as it did on Friday, that is a good exchange; if CrowdStrike's valuation falls toward Zscaler's, the stake shrinks with it.

The first test came before the bell. CrowdStrike was down 8.0% at $211.10 at 8:37 a.m. Eastern, Nasdaq pre-market data show, which values the offer at about $239.60 a Zscaler share, a 23.0% premium rather than the 34% announced. Zscaler was up 19.4% at $232.60, 3.0% below that value, as TECHi reported on the deal.

What does it mean for shareholders?

For CrowdStrike's owners, the arithmetic is attractive on paper: they keep about 84% of a company that adds about 62% to their own recurring revenue and 88% to their quarterly free cash flow. The risks are integration, a year or more of waiting for approvals, and paying in shares at a time when the market is marking those shares down.

For Zscaler's owners, the quarter is a reminder of what they are giving up: a business that turns more of each dollar of revenue into cash than its buyer does. TECHi reported in September that both stocks rose as investors treated security as a beneficiary of AI spending. Its quarterly report and the proxy statement for the shareholder vote come next.

What to watch

The open at 9:30 a.m., and whether Zscaler's gap to the value of the offer narrows. Zscaler's quarterly report, due within 40 days of the quarter's end, which will carry its own account of the deal's risks. The proxy statement, which will set out the background to the deal and the advisers' valuation work, and the antitrust filings. TECHi's CrowdStrike quote page carries the live price.

data.title: AI hardware stocks lose 19.5% in a week; Nvidia falls 14% after SEC probe report
data.description:
Ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks fell 11.4% on average on Friday, November 20, 2026, and ended the week 19.5% lower, Nasdaq closing prices show. That is the group's largest weekly fall in a series that starts in March 2025. All ten fell on the day and all ten fell on the week.

It was the third week in six in which the group lost about 15% or more: 16.9% in the week to October 16, 15.0% in the week to November 6, and 19.5% now. TECHi's calculation shows the ten are down 38.0% on average since October 9. Nvidia, which is not part of that average, fell 14.0% to $125.53 after Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is examining its accounting. It was the stock's seventh fall in a row.

How did Friday end?

Lower than it began. The ten were down 4.8% on average before the opening bell, as TECHi's pre-market report showed. They closed down 11.4%. None of the ten closed above its early price.

That report set a marker for the day: whether the group would close above its morning level. It did not.

The largest falls were at Micron (13.9%), AMD (13.2%) and Broadcom (12.2%). Super Micro fell least, 9.2%. The Nasdaq Composite, a broad index of the stocks listed on that exchange, fell 5.3% on the day and 10.0% on the week.

Nvidia closed at $125.53, down 14.0%. It was the stock's largest one-day fall since January 27, 2025, and its lowest close since May 12, 2025. On the 24.1 billion shares it has outstanding, the company ended the day worth $3.03 trillion. Alphabet, on the share counts in its latest quarterly report, ended at $3.25 trillion. TECHi reported the crossover earlier on Friday, when Nvidia's two-week loss of market value stood at about $1.2 trillion. At the close it was $1.47 trillion.

How have the morning readings held up?

Poorly, three days running. TECHi has taken a reading of the same ten stocks before the open on each of the last three sessions and compared it with the close.

On Wednesday the group was up 4.0% before the bell and finished up 0.7%. On Thursday it was up 3.9% and finished down 3.5%. On Friday it was down 4.8% and finished down 11.4%. The close fell short of the morning by 3.3 points, then 7.4 points, then 6.6 points.

Three sessions do not make a rule. They do show that early prices in these stocks, which come from thin trading, have been a poor guide to where the day ends.

How bad was the week?

The ten are Broadcom, AMD, Arista Networks, Vertiv, Super Micro, TSMC, Micron, Marvell, Dell and CoreWeave. The average is unweighted, so a small company counts as much as a large one.

The group fell on four of the five days. It lost 6.2% on Monday, when all ten fell, and 0.2% on Tuesday. It gained 0.7% on Wednesday, the day after Nvidia's results. It lost 3.5% on Thursday, when all ten fell again, and 11.4% on Friday.

No stock escaped. The weakest over the week were CoreWeave (25.6%), Micron (23.6%), Marvell (22.0%) and AMD (20.5%). Broadcom fell least, 12.3%.

Nvidia lost 22.9% on the week, a little more than the group. The week before, it had fallen while the others rose. It has now fallen for seven weeks in a row, the longest run of weekly losses in the prices TECHi checked, which go back to August 2024. The longest before this one lasted four weeks.

How does it compare with earlier weeks?

TECHi's series for the ten begins on March 28, 2025, the day CoreWeave started trading, and now covers 86 weeks. Three of the four largest weekly falls in it have come since the start of October. The fourth was the week to April 4, 2025, when the group lost 14.2%. In all, the group has lost 10% or more in a week five times, and three of those weeks fall in the last six.

The sequence matters as much as the size. The group fell 16.9% in the week to October 16 and 15.0% in the week to November 6. Two quieter weeks sat between them, with losses of 1.8% and 0.5%. The group then rose 10.6% in the week to November 13. That was the week Nvidia's chief executive resigned and its shares fell 12.8%, and the rest of the group went the other way. This week they fell together.

Put the six weeks together and the ten are down 38.0% on average since October 9. A stock that falls by that much has to rise 61.4% to get back.

Which stocks are at their lowest?

Seven of the ten closed on Friday at prices they had not seen since May or earlier. Each is at its lowest close since the date given: CoreWeave since April 22, 2025; Vertiv since January 9; Super Micro since March 30; TSMC since March 30; Marvell since April 9; Micron since May 4; Dell since May 21.

The other three have been lower more recently. Broadcom, AMD and Arista Networks all closed below Friday's level at some point this month.

CoreWeave's is the oldest mark. Its close of $39.51 is below every close since its first month of trading.

Since October 9 the largest losses are at Marvell (55.6%), Dell (52.6%), CoreWeave (51.9%) and Super Micro (48.3%). Broadcom has held up best, down 15.8%.

What about the companies that buy the hardware?

They fell less. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta fell 3.9% on average on Friday and lost 9.5% over the week. Since October 9 they are down 15.5%, against 38.0% for the hardware stocks.

Over the week Meta lost 12.6%, Alphabet lost 10.3%, Microsoft lost 7.5% and Amazon 7.4%.

That gap has been the pattern of the whole decline. The companies spending on AI have lost some of their value. The companies they buy from have lost more than a third of theirs.

What is behind it?

Two reports landed on Friday, at the end of a week that was already going badly. TECHi has not established how much of the fall each one explains, and prices do not say.

Reuters reported on Friday afternoon, citing two people briefed on the matter, that the SEC is examining Nvidia's accounting practices. The Wall Street Journal had reported an SEC investigation on Tuesday without saying what it covered. Reuters said it could not determine when the inquiry opened or which accounting issues are involved. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment, and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing, and Reuters noted that many close without any enforcement action.

Broadcom fell 12.2%. Ming-Chi Kuo, an analyst at TF International Securities, wrote on Friday that his industry survey shows Google cutting its 2027 shipments of an AI chip series that Broadcom designs for it by about a fifth, according to accounts of his note in the financial press. Neither company has commented.

Those came on top of the week's other events. Nvidia reported results on Tuesday. A US rule limiting exports of advanced AI chips took effect on Thursday. Nvidia still has an interim chief executive and a board investigation it has not described.

What the numbers show is that the selling was not confined to Nvidia or Broadcom. On Monday, Thursday and Friday every one of the ten fell. Memory, networking, servers and rented computing capacity all went down together, which is what a change of mind about the whole sector looks like, and not a judgment on one company.

What does it mean for shareholders?

Two readings are available. One is that prices have moved further than the reported numbers. Nvidia's forecast for this quarter, given on Tuesday, is higher than its sales last quarter, and its interim chief executive told analysts that demand far exceeds supply, CBS News reported. The other is that investors are changing their minds about how much AI hardware will be bought, and at what profit, in the years after that. Prices alone cannot settle which is right. The next round of quarterly results will add evidence. A reported regulatory inquiry into the sector's largest company is a different kind of risk, and results will not resolve it.

What to watch

Any statement from Nvidia or the SEC on the reported inquiry. Any comment from Google or Broadcom on next year's chip orders. Monday's pre-market readings, which TECHi will measure against Friday's close, and whether Nvidia's run of declines reaches eight. Jensen Huang is due to give a transcribed interview to three House committees on December 1, the Foreign Affairs Committee has said, and Nvidia's quarterly report is due by December 4. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom carry live prices.

data.title: Premarket: AI hardware stocks up 7.4% after Friday's rout; Nvidia up 9.4%
data.description:
AI hardware stocks were higher before Monday's opening bell, after their worst week in TECHi's records. Ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks were up 7.4% on average at 4:30 a.m. Eastern on Monday, November 23, 2026, against Friday's closing prices, Nasdaq pre-market data show, with all ten higher. Nvidia was up 9.4% at $137.35.

On average that would win back about 59% of the ground each stock lost on Friday, when the group fell 11.4%, TECHi's calculation shows. Nvidia's reading regains about 58% of its 14.0% drop. Last week, mornings were a poor guide: on each of the last three sessions, the group closed below its pre-market level.

How are AI stocks trading before the bell?

Higher across the board. Among the ten hardware stocks, CoreWeave was up 9.6%, Dell 8.6%, TSMC 8.2%, Super Micro 7.7%, Marvell 7.5%, Micron 7.4%, AMD 6.7%, Broadcom 6.3%, Vertiv 6.2% and Arista Networks 6.1%. CoreWeave led and Arista Networks lagged. The four largest buyers of AI hardware were up 4.1% on average: Alphabet was up 4.9%, Meta 4.3%, Amazon 4.0% and Microsoft 3.1%.

Nasdaq-100 futures were up 3.8% at 4:20 a.m. Eastern, and S&P 500 futures 2.9%. Pre-market trading is thin, and prices before 9:30 a.m. can move sharply on small orders.

How much of Friday's fall would that recover?

A little more than half. On Friday the ten fell 11.4% on average, the third-largest one-day fall in TECHi's daily series for the group, which starts in March 2025, as TECHi reported after the close. Only November 5 of this year and April 3, 2025 were worse. A 7.4% average gain from Friday's close still leaves the group below where it was on Thursday, because a fall and an equal rise are not the same distance: on average the ten need about 13% to get all the way back.

Nvidia shows the same arithmetic. It closed at $125.53 on Friday after falling 14.0%. Thursday's close of $145.98 was 16.3% above that, so a stock that falls 14% needs to rise about 16.3% to get back. The pre-market reading of $137.35 covers 58% of that distance.

Nvidia lost 22.9% last week, its seventh weekly fall in a row. At Monday's reading it is still 15.7% below its close of November 13.

What are the futures saying?

That the wider market is set to recover some of Friday's ground as well. The Nasdaq-100 index fell 5.6% on Friday. A rise matching the 3.8% in its futures would take back about 63% of that fall, TECHi's calculation shows, though futures and the index are not priced identically. S&P 500 futures were up 2.9%.

The futures move came overnight, as Asian markets traded. It was already visible on Sunday evening, when Nasdaq-100 futures opened higher.

Which stocks are bouncing most?

Measured by how much of Friday's drop each has made back, TSMC 78%, Super Micro 76% and CoreWeave 70% were in front. Micron 46%, Broadcom 45% and AMD 44% were behind. Dell reports quarterly results on Tuesday, and its shares fell 11.0% on Friday. All ten were above Friday’s close and all ten were still below Thursday’s, so none has yet made back the whole of Friday.

The four buyers fell less on Friday, so smaller gains take them further. Microsoft and Alphabet were trading above their Thursday closes before the bell, so for them Friday’s loss is already made up on paper.

Where does that leave Nvidia against Alphabet?

Close. On Friday afternoon Nvidia's market value fell below Alphabet's, as TECHi reported, and at Friday's close Nvidia was worth about $3.03 trillion. At the pre-market price Nvidia would be worth about $3.31 trillion on its 24.1 billion shares, and Alphabet about $3.41 trillion on the share counts in its latest quarterly report, which would leave Nvidia behind by about $100 billion. These are pre-market prices, and the gap can change by tens of billions of dollars in minutes.

What happened over the weekend?

Asian markets had the first say. In Taipei, TSMC's shares rose 1.5% and the Taiex 2.2% on the first day of new limits on short selling, as TECHi reported overnight. In Seoul the main index fell 3.3%, even as customs data showed South Korea's chip exports reaching a record $38.5 billion in the first 20 days of November, as TECHi also reported.

Taiwan's financial regulator barred short sales below the previous day's close from Monday and raised the margin required on short positions to 150% from 130%. In Seoul, the finance minister said the government had a contingency plan beyond a market stabilization fund the authorities agreed on Sunday to prepare, Yonhap reported.

Two reports from Friday afternoon still hang over the group. Reuters reported, citing two people briefed on the matter, that the Securities and Exchange Commission is examining Nvidia's accounting practices. An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing, and Reuters said many close without enforcement action. An analyst's note said Google was cutting 2027 orders for an AI chip that Broadcom designs for it. Neither company had commented on that note.

What does TSMC's US price say?

That some of Friday's gap with Taipei is closing. TSMC's US shares were up 8.2% before the bell at $344.80. At Monday's Taipei close of NT$2,030 and the current exchange rate, that is 11.6% above the value of the five Taiwan shares each US share represents. On Friday the gap was 5.0%, against a median of 18.6% over the past two years and 11.5% in November. That is close to the November median, and still well below the two-year median, so the US shares carry less of a premium than they usually do.

How reliable are the morning readings?

Not very, lately. TECHi has measured the same ten stocks before the open on each of the last four sessions. On Wednesday the group was up 4.0% before the bell and closed up 0.7%. On Thursday it was up 3.9% and closed down 3.5%. On Friday it was down 4.8% and closed down 11.4%, as TECHi's pre-market report and closing report showed.

Each time the close was worse than the morning, by 3.3 points, then 7.4 points, then 6.6 points. Three sessions do not make a rule, and the direction of the morning changed between them. What they show is that early prices in these stocks have been a poor forecast of where the day ends.

What does it mean for shareholders?

A higher morning is not a recovery. On average the ten would need to rise about 13% from Friday's close just to get back to Thursday's prices, and last week's losses were spread across memory, networking, servers and chip foundries alike.

There is a case that the selling went too far. Nvidia's latest forecast is higher than its last quarter's sales, and Korea's export data show chip demand still growing. There is also a case that it did not. The reported SEC inquiry into the industry's largest company is a new kind of risk, and the group has lost about 38% on average since October 9.

What to watch

The open, and whether the group closes above its pre-market level for the first time in four sessions. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, a server maker, reports after the close on Monday, and Dell reports on Tuesday, according to Nasdaq's earnings calendar. Any statement from Nvidia or the SEC on the reported inquiry. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Trump asks Nvidia’s board to rehire Huang, five days after it ruled out his return
data.description:
President Donald Trump said on Sunday night that he hopes Nvidia's board rehires Jensen Huang, five days after the board's chair said it did not intend to reinstate him as chief executive. "It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social at 9:54 p.m. Eastern on November 22, 2026.

Nvidia's shares were up 8.2% at $135.85 at 5:45 a.m. Eastern on Monday, before the market opened, against Friday's close of $125.53, Nasdaq pre-market data show. About 44% of that rise had already happened by 8 p.m. on Friday, two days before the post. After it, Nvidia gained 0.9 percentage points more than ten other AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks, a difference worth about $27 billion of market value, TECHi's calculation shows. That is the most the post could explain, not a measure of its effect.

What did Trump write?

Two sentences. The post says Trump hopes the board rehires Huang, and that doing so would be the best thing for the company and for the country. It does not say whether he has spoken to Huang or to any director, and it gives no other reason.

TECHi read the text of the 120 posts on Trump's account from 8:42 a.m. Eastern on November 15 to Monday morning. This is the only one that names Nvidia or Huang, though many of the others are images, which a text search cannot read. Nvidia had not responded publicly by 5:43 a.m. Eastern on Monday: its newsroom showed no release since Thursday, and it had filed nothing with the Securities and Exchange Commission since the post.

What has Nvidia's board said about Huang?

That he is not coming back. On November 11 the board accepted Huang's resignation as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately, according to Nvidia's filing with the SEC. It made Colette Kress, the chief financial officer since 2013, interim chief executive, and appointed Harvey Jones, a director since 1993, as chair.

Jones opened the earnings call on November 17 by saying the board had accepted the resignation unanimously and did not intend to reinstate Huang as chief executive, as TECHi reported from accounts of the call by CNBC and CBS News. The board has hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles and is considering candidates from inside and outside the company. Hours before the call, Huang had said he would return if the board decided that was in the company's interest, CBS News reported.

Nvidia's own statements give no reason for the resignation. Reuters has reported that Huang stepped down over extramarital relationships, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. On November 10, the day before the board accepted his resignation, its independent directors said they had hired Joon H. Kim, a former acting US attorney in Manhattan, and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run an investigation, as TECHi reported at the time. Nvidia has not given a date for its findings.

Who decides whether Huang comes back?

The board does. It accepted the resignation, chose the interim chief executive and hired the search firm, and Huang is no longer a director. Shareholders elect the directors, but their next scheduled vote is at the annual meeting, which Nvidia held in June this year. The President has no formal part in the choice.

Nothing in Trump's post changes that process. What it adds is a public view from the President on a decision the board says it has already made, while the investigation the board commissioned is still under way.

Did the post move Nvidia's shares?

Less than Monday's price suggests. Nvidia closed at $125.53 on Friday after falling 14.0% following a Reuters report about the SEC, as TECHi reported. In after-hours trading, which ended at 8 p.m., it recovered to $130.03, up 3.6%. The ten other AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks rose 2.9% on average in the same session.

From Friday's last after-hours trade to Monday's pre-market reading, Nvidia rose a further 4.5%, against 3.6% for the ten. The difference, 0.9 points, is worth about $27 billion at Nvidia's 24.1 billion shares. That window also includes Monday's trading in Asia, where Taipei rose and Seoul fell, and a 3.4% rise in Nasdaq-100 futures, so the difference is the most the post could explain, not a measure of its effect.

Pre-market trading is thin, and these prices can move sharply on small orders before the 9:30 a.m. open. TECHi's pre-market report has the full board for the group.

How does it fit with Bessent's call for an outsider?

It points the other way. On November 15 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News that the board should look outside the company as it searches for a new leader, and that he wanted answers from the board and its outside counsel within 10 days, Axios reported. Ten days from that appearance is Wednesday, November 25.

Bessent also questioned whether sales to China had inflated Nvidia's results, according to the same report, and Nvidia did not respond at the time. Five days later Reuters reported that the SEC's enforcement staff is examining potential accounting issues at the company, citing two people familiar with the matter. An examination is not a finding of wrongdoing, and Nvidia has not confirmed it.

So within a week, the President and his Treasury Secretary have both said publicly who should run Nvidia, and they point in different directions. The board has followed neither so far: it has not named an outsider, and it has said Huang will not return.

How much value has Nvidia lost since Huang left?

About $1.16 trillion, measured from the close on November 11, the day the board accepted the resignation, to Friday's close, a fall of 27.7%. From November 6, the last close before the investigation was announced, the loss is 32.7%, or about $1.47 trillion. The ten other hardware stocks fell 23.6% on average from November 11 to Friday, so Nvidia trailed them by 4.1 points. Most of Nvidia's fall since Huang left, in other words, came with the rest of the group; the part that is Nvidia's alone is closer to 4.1 points, or about $174 billion. Nvidia's troubles may also have weighed on the companies that supply it, so the split is rough.

Monday's pre-market price would win back about $249 billion of that if it held at the open. It would still leave Nvidia 21.8% below its November 11 close.

What else is pending?

Three things. Huang has agreed to appear before House lawmakers on December 1, CBS News reported. Nvidia's quarterly report is due by December 4, and it is where the company describes legal proceedings and could say whether it has received any inquiry from the SEC. The board has not said when the investigation led by Kim will report.

What does it mean for shareholders?

A post is not a decision. The board has said once, on the record, that Huang will not return, and nothing Nvidia has filed since has changed that. If it reversed itself, investors would be weighing the founder's return against the findings of an investigation that has not yet reported.

There are two readings of Monday's price. One is that some investors now see a path back for Huang and value it. The other is that most of the rise had other causes: a rebound across AI hardware stocks after their worst week in TECHi's records, and higher futures overnight. The calculation above favours the second, since much of Nvidia's move came before the post and most of the rest matched its peers. It cannot rule out the first.

What to watch

Whether Nvidia or its board answers the post, and whether the board says anything by Wednesday, when Bessent's 10 days run out. The open at 9:30 a.m., and whether Nvidia's lead over its peers holds once the regular session begins. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Elastic beats its forecast by $9M, keeps its full-year target; the dollar costs $9.5M
data.description:
Elastic, the search and data software company, reported revenue of $495.9 million for the three months to October 31, 2026, up 17% from a year earlier and $8.9 million above the top of its own forecast, according to results released after the market closed on Thursday, November 19. It did not raise its revenue target for the full year. The midpoint stays at $2.004 billion.

The reason is the dollar. Elastic said a stronger dollar will take $9.5 million off revenue in the second half of its fiscal year, which is almost exactly the $9.4 million by which the latest quarter beat the middle of its forecast, TECHi's calculation shows. The forecast for the current quarter points to growth of 12.9%, down from 17.1%. The shares closed at $75.17 on Friday, down 1.5%, on a day when the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3%.

How did Elastic do against its forecast?

It beat it on every measure it guides. Elastic sells software that companies use to search their own data, monitor their systems and detect security threats, and it has been rebuilding its products around AI.

In August the company told investors to expect revenue of $486 million to $487 million and adjusted earnings of 80 to 82 cents a share. Revenue was $495.9 million. Adjusted earnings were 94 cents a share, 12 cents above the top of the range. The adjusted operating margin was 22.2%, against a forecast of about 19.0%.

Subscription revenue from customers signed by its sales teams, the figure Elastic treats as its core, rose 19% to $415 million. On the standard accounting measure the company made an operating profit of $22 million, after a loss of $24 million in the previous quarter.

The number of customers paying more than $100,000 a year rose to more than 1,830, from more than 1,800 three months earlier and more than 1,600 a year earlier.

Why didn't the full-year target go up?

Because the gain was offset by exchange rates. Elastic reports in dollars and earns part of its revenue in euros and pounds.

When it last gave a forecast, in August, it assumed a euro worth about $1.17 and a pound worth about $1.36. It now assumes $1.09 and $1.31. A stronger dollar makes each euro of revenue worth fewer dollars. The company puts the cost at $4.5 million in the current quarter and $5.0 million in the one after, $9.5 million in all.

The old full-year range was $1.998 billion to $2.010 billion. The new one is $2.000 billion to $2.008 billion. Both have a midpoint of $2.004 billion.

So the beat was absorbed. Measured without currency moves, the picture is better: Elastic now expects growth of 15.9% for the year at constant exchange rates, where in August it expected 15.3%. The profit forecast did rise. Adjusted earnings for the year are now expected to be $3.35 to $3.41 a share, up from $3.29 to $3.37.

What does the forecast imply for growth?

A dip and then a partial recovery. For the quarter to the end of January, Elastic expects revenue of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That is 12.9% more than a year earlier, or 13.9% without the currency effect, and 2.4% more than the quarter just reported.

The full-year target then implies something for the final quarter. Subtract the first half and the midpoint of the current quarter's forecast from $2.004 billion and $521.9 million is left. That would be growth of 15.7% on a year earlier.

Set out in order, the year-on-year growth rates run 15% in the first quarter, 17% in the second, 12.9% forecast for the third and 15.7% implied for the fourth.

The company's record makes the forecasts look cautious. Revenue has come in above its range in both quarters of this fiscal year. In the first it was $478 million against a forecast of $469 million to $470 million, and in the second $495.9 million against $486 million to $487 million.

Elastic kept two other targets roughly where they were. It still expects adjusted free cash flow of about 21.5% of revenue for the year, and it nudged its adjusted operating margin target to about 19.5% from 19.4%.

What do the contract figures show?

Less momentum than the revenue line. Remaining performance obligations, the value of signed contracts not yet counted as revenue, were $1.858 billion, up 23% from a year earlier. The part due within twelve months was $1.157 billion, up 19%.

Against the previous quarter both were almost flat. The total rose 0.2% from $1.854 billion and the twelve-month figure 0.3% from $1.153 billion. The total is 6.3% below the $1.982 billion reported at the end of April, the close of Elastic's last fiscal year.

Year-on-year growth in the twelve-month figure slowed to 19% from 21% a quarter earlier. Cash generation was also lighter. Operating cash flow was $44 million, against $132 million in the previous quarter.

What is Elastic doing in AI?

Adding AI agents to its existing products and buying its way into a new one. The release lists an agent that investigates system faults, a set of agents that sort and investigate security alerts, and a serverless version of its vector database, the kind of store that AI applications use to find relevant text.

It also announced an agreement to buy HoneyHive, a young company whose software monitors and tests AI agents. The release gives no price.

These are the company's descriptions of its own products. The release does not say how much revenue comes from AI features.

What about buybacks?

Elastic bought back about 0.6 million shares in the quarter at an average price of $86.31, spending about $55 million. Its board approved a new $500 million program on November 17, which includes about $45 million left over from the old one and has no expiration date.

Thursday's close of $76.33 was 11.6% below the average price paid in the quarter. At Friday's close the new program equals 6.1% of the company's market value.

How did the stock react?

Elastic closed at $76.33 on Thursday, down 8.0% on the day, before the results came out. On Friday the shares closed at $75.17, down 1.5%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% the same day.

That is unusually calm for this stock. On the day after each of its last four reports it moved by more than 12%: down 14.7% last November, down 15.4% in February, up 12.3% in May and up 19.3% in August.

The shares are 29.5% below their closing high of $106.58, set on October 28, and about level with where they started the year. At Friday's close the company was worth about $8.2 billion, 4.1 times the revenue it forecasts for this fiscal year and about 22 times forecast adjusted earnings.

There is a case on each side. Elastic keeps beating its own forecasts, it is profitable on the standard accounting measure, and it is buying back stock. Against that, the forecast shows growth slowing next quarter, contract totals were flat on the quarter, and the wider market fell sharply on Friday.

What to watch

Whether revenue for the January quarter lands above $508.5 million, as it has landed above the range in each quarter this year. The contract figures, which need to grow again for the fourth-quarter target to look safe. The price and timing of the HoneyHive purchase. The euro and the pound, which have now cost Elastic a forecast increase.
